articles.title: This AI Radio Host Speaks Spanish and Backs Immigrants. It’s Winning Over Listeners
articles.summary: Coyotec is bilingual, swears, and tells listeners how to defend themselves against ICE. Its popularity comes as more broadcasters are experimenting with artificial personalities.
body: As footage of ICE raids, deportations, and protests flooded social media feeds throughout the summer of 2025 and into the following year, Eduardo Maytorena wasn’t sure what his team should do.

At the time, Maytorena was the LA station general manager for the broadcasting giant Entravision, which features programming in Spanish and English for Latino audiences. He and his fellow leaders were looking to the company's on-air personalities to say something in support of immigrants, but they realized how high the stakes were and how dangerous the situation was.
"We just felt really helpless," Maytorena, now Entravision's president of audio, says.
But there was one host who could offer Entravision’s audiences solace and speak freely without facing consequences—because it’s an artificially intelligent avatar.

articles.title: Valve Steam Frame Review: Costly and Inconsistent
articles.summary: The Steam Frame’s promise of greatness for stand-alone and streaming VR gaming doesn’t quite connect.
body: Valve has had a complicated relationship with virtual reality gaming. Its Steam client—the number one distribution platform for PC games—has long supported VR titles and works with headsets from other manufacturers. But the company's flagship VR headset, 2019’s Valve Index, never quite escaped its niche. It saw a huge sales spike in the run-up to the release of headline title Half-Life: Alyx, but by February 2025, it accounted for only 13.2 percent of VR headsets used on Steam.

Enter the Steam Frame, Valve’s second attempt at snatching the VR gaming crown. More than a hardware refresh, it promises to reimagine PC VR gaming, operating as a stand-alone headset like the Meta Quest 3, the current reigning champion, while letting users seamlessly stream games from a more powerful remote machine. It mostly succeeds—but a few issues hold it back.

Specs-wise, the Steam Frame is one of the better VR headsets, though far from a powerhouse. It packs a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chip—a slightly dated offering, having debuted in 2023—with 16 GB of RAM, and either 256 GB (at the $1,059 price) or 1 TB ($1,299) of storage, plus a microSD slot for expansion, allowing it to install and run games locally.
points: The Steam Frame’s promise of greatness for stand-alone and streaming VR gaming doesn’t quite connect.

articles.title: A YouTuber dissected an iPhone Duo and thinks he found the cause of crackgate
articles.summary: Social media and the iPhone Duo subreddit are filled with reports of Apple's foldable failing quickly and in spectacular fashion. Some users report having the phone for only a few hours before the hinge seems to catch on something, then audibly crack and break the screen.
body: A weak spot in the hinge may be failing and cracking iPhone Duo screens.

YouTuber CuriousHagi was able to reproduce the cracked screen during some durability testing of the iPhone Duo. Then he pulled it apart to try and find the culprit. What he found is that the Duo’s hinge is quite complex, consisting of a gear-like central hinge and two different types of linking hinges.

The piece that broke is one of the links in the middle of the phone that happens to be thinner than the links below or above it, and it snapped at a small notch where it would be weakest. He also found marks where the hinge met the support plate, indicating where it may have gotten caught.

articles.title: Anthropic sued for allegedly using 274 Elvis Presley songs to train AI models
articles.summary: Authentic Brands Group says AI company infringed on rights of songs by the King such as Can’t Help Falling in Love. The owners of Elvis Presley ’s music catalogue are suing artificial intelligence ( AI ) company Anthropic for allegedly using Presley’s songs to train their models without permission.
body: Authentic Brands Group, the licensing organization that has ownership of both Presley’s music and likeness, is accusing Anthropic of infringing on the rights of 274 songs by Presley. The lawsuit, first reported by Billboard, was filed on Friday.

While AI firms have already faced copyright infringement claims from the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and music labels such as Sony, Universal and Warner Records, this case represents one of the first major legal challenges brought directly by an artist’s estate against an AI developer. The result could set a broader precedent for how AI companies are allowed to use existing music catalogues.

“The Elvis plaintiffs bring this action to enforce these exclusive rights against the defendant that has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before,” lead attorney Richard Busch wrote in the lawsuit.

The lawsuit claims that “from its inception, Anthropic’s AI model, ‘Claude,’ has created infringing output of copyrighted material of virtually every song from every catalog available on the internet”.

articles.title: Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing
articles.summary: Data centres are the lifeblood of our digital world, but there are growing concerns about their environmental impact. The BBC explores their rise in charts.
body: Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was.
These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking.
They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude.
But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world.

articles.title: iFixit’s look inside the iPhone Duo may explain those broken screens and hinges
articles.summary: As is tradition, iFixit has torn open the latest iPhone and laid its parts bare on a table. It found some interesting details about how Apple might be hiding the crease on the Duo's folding screen and gave it a 5/10 repairability score.
body: The iPhone Duo is the most repairable foldable yet, but that’s not saying much.

The internal screen’s matte nano-texture cover doesn’t just make it more readable in bright sunlight; it also helps mask the crease by scattering reflections. When looking at the display under a microscope, iFixit also found oval-shaped subpixels arranged at various angles, which the site believes are designed to reduce artifacts and further mask the crease down the middle of the display.

The nano-texture outer layer is relatively easy to replace without swapping out the OLED underneath. If you do need to repair the display itself, however, good luck. As is the case with other foldables, it’s an expensive nightmare. Dust did make it into the USB-C port, speaker grills, and the hinge — making it a bit crunchy. But noticeably less of the glow dust found its way inside the phone than the Z Fold8 or Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

articles.title: Scott Walker’s The Drift will get under your skin
articles.summary: In my mind, Spooky Season music comes in two distinct flavors. There are the fun, occasionally goofy songs like "The Monster Mash" and John Carpenter's "Halloween Theme." Then there is the genuinely terrifying: Throbbing Gristle, The Body, or Scott Walker's The Drift.
body: Walker’s 2006 album is unsettling, bizarre, and the perfect way to kill a party.

This 2006 album from the singer-songwriter is truly upsetting. On it, Walker explores death, disease, and tragedy. But not just from some abstract perspective. There are visceral descriptions of the hanging of Benito Mussolini and his mistress Clara Petacci. He sings about 9/11, his stillborn twin brother, and the Srebrenica genocide. Lyrically, it’s about as dark as an album gets.

At times, the record sounds more like the score to an Ari Aster film than anything that could be called pop music under even the most generous definitions. Seasick guitars in the verses of “Jesse” give way to dissonant strings that drone oppressively over the chorus. You can feel the low-bitrate MP3 noise that opens “Clara” in your jaw, which also allegedly features the sound of his percussionist punching a pig carcass as part of the rhythm track.

articles.title: ‘Extremely disappointed’: WA government seeks reimbursement from Deloitte over flawed university report
articles.summary: State paid consultancy firm $166,000 for feasibility study on merging the three tertiary institutions. Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast. The Western Australian government has said it is “extremely disappointed” and is seeking an “expedited” cost recovery from Deloitte…
body: The government paid Deloitte $166,000 for a feasibility study on merging the University of Western Australia, Curtin University and Murdoch University.
Deloitte considered three merger options between the three universities, with “low”, “mid” and “high” cost scenarios, and broke down the calculations of those costs in the report’s appendix.

Under the “high” cost scenario of a merger between Curtin and UWA, the report calculates the “total costs to day 1” as $514m, and “post day 1” over five years at $145m. The total cost of those two payments is $659m but the report wrote $399m – a $260m discrepancy.

Prof Stephen Bartos, an expert in public sector governance at the University of Canberra, said the errors discredited the report. “In my view, they’re so extensive that you probably need a new report, or at the very least someone to go through that material from the ground up and rework it manually without the use of AI,” he said.
